lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Say French vowels and key sounds clearly and greet patients formally at the bedside.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Greet a patient at the bedside, say your name and that you are their nurse, and ask how they are using vous.

items.note: A man who is a nurse is l'infirmier. In- is nasal: an-feer-MYEHR.
Use la patiente for a woman. The final t is silent and -ent is nasal: pah-SYAHN.
The final t is silent: lee. Note the gender: le lit.
Ain is a nasal vowel, never pronounced as an n: MAN.
The u is silent and in is nasal: suh-RANG.
Ill sounds like y and the final r is silent: lo-ray-YAY.
-euil sounds like 'uhy', and the final t is silent: fo-TUHY roo-LAHN.
Oi sounds like wa: pwa-TREEN.
Ch is sh and am is nasal: SHAHM-bruh. L'habitation means housing, not a hospital room.
The middle e is almost silent and -cin is nasal: mayd-SAN. Same word for a woman.
The French r is made at the back of the throat, never rolled: dya-RAY.
Votre = your (formal). A man says je suis votre infirmier. J is the s in measure: zhuh.
J is the s in measure, and -elle rhymes with bell: zhuh ma-PEL AN.
Use vous with patients and families. Liaison: the t of comment links to allez, and the z of allez stays silent: ko-mahn-ta-lay-VOO.
Enchanté if you are a man. En- is nasal: ahn-shahn-TAY.
Bonne nuit only when leaving at night; to greet in the evening say Bonsoir.

passage.target: Anne est l'infirmière de la chambre 12.
passage.native: Anne is the nurse for room 12.

passage.target: Mme Rouget est la patiente du lit 2.

passage.native: Anne: Good morning, I'm your nurse.

passage.target: Anne : Enchantée, Madame.
passage.native: Anne: Nice to meet you, ma'am.

passage.target: Anne : Comment allez-vous ?
passage.native: Anne: How are you?

passage.target: Mme Rouget : J'ai la diarrhée et j'ai mal à la poitrine.
passage.native: Mrs. Rouget: I have diarrhea and my chest hurts.

passage.target: Anne lui prend la main et arrange l'oreiller.
passage.native: Anne takes her hand and fixes the pillow.

passage.target: Anne met la seringue neuve sur la table.
passage.native: Anne puts the new syringe on the table.

passage.target: Anne appelle le médecin et approche le fauteuil roulant.
passage.native: Anne calls the doctor and brings the wheelchair closer.

example.target: Bonjour, je suis votre infirmière.
example.native: Good morning, I'm your nurse.

verbs.note: Irregular. Use être to say who you are and what your job is: no article before a job (je suis infirmière). Votre infirmière is the formal (vous) way to say your nurse.

verbs.native: to go; to be (how someone is doing)

example.target: Comment allez-vous ?
example.native: How are you?

verbs.note: Irregular. French uses aller, not être, to ask how someone is: Comment allez-vous ? Use allez with a patient (formal vous), and vas only with a colleague you call tu.

example.target: J'ai la diarrhée et j'ai mal à la poitrine.
example.native: I have diarrhea and my chest hurts.

verbs.note: Irregular. Je becomes j' before a vowel: j'ai. Patients use avoir mal à to tell you where it hurts.

example.target: Anne appelle le médecin.
example.native: Anne calls the doctor.

verbs.note: Spelling change: the l doubles in appelle but not in appelons or appelez. The reflexive form gives you Je m'appelle Anne (My name is Anne). Practice the -elle sound here: a-PEL.

example.target: Anne met la seringue neuve sur la table.
example.native: Anne puts the new syringe on the table.

verbs.note: Irregular. The final t of met is silent in the singular: meh. Nurses also say poser for putting something down.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say numbers, clock times and vital sign readings in degrees, kilos, mg and mL.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Tell a patient the time and read their temperature, pulse and blood pressure numbers out loud in French.

items.note: The h is silent: l'heure sounds like LUHR.
The final -mme sounds like a single m: mee-lee-GRAM.
Ill sounds like eel here: mee-lee-LEE-truh.
Short for le kilogramme. France weighs in kilos; 165 pounds is about 75 kilos.
Oi sounds like wa and the final ds is silent: pwa.
Final -ure is the French u (lips rounded, say ee): tahn-pay-ra-TUR.
Stress falls on the last syllable: duh-GRAY.
Short for la tension artérielle. French nurses say blood pressure in cmHg: 120/80 is douze-huit, 12/8.
The l and s are silent: poo.
Patients also say le cachet. Com- is nasal: kohn-pree-MAY.
Regular plural: les doses. Pronounced dohz.
Il est une heure for one o'clock, il est … heures for the others.
In French decimals use a comma: 36,7 (trente-six sept).
Say it in cmHg: douze-huit. Use à with a reading: la tension est à 12/8.
Soixante-douze: oi is wa, and the x of soixante sounds like s: swa-sahnt-DOOZ.

items.target: D'après la prescription médicale, vous devez prendre 1 comprimé à 9 h.
items.native: Per the doctor's order, you're due for 1 pill at 9.
items.note: Vous devez prendre = you're due to take. Say à neuf heures.
Always read the amount back from the label or order. Say cinq millilitres.

passage.target: Dans la chambre 214, M. Roux demande l'heure.
passage.native: In room 214, Mr. Roux asks the time.

passage.native: Anne: Your weight today is 75 kilos.

passage.native: Anne confirms the dose: per the doctor's order, it is 500 milligrams.

passage.target: Anne : D'après la prescription médicale, vous devez prendre 1 comprimé à 9 h.
passage.native: Anne: Per the doctor's order, you're due for 1 pill at 9.

example.native: Your temperature is 36.7 degrees.

verbs.note: Irregular. Use il est for clock time (Il est 8 heures) and est de or est à for readings.

example.target: L'étiquette indique 5 millilitres.
example.native: The label says 5 milliliters.

verbs.note: Regular -er verb. Useful for reading back an order or a label. The -que ending is pronounced k.

example.target: Anne confirme la dose.
example.native: Anne confirms the dose.

verbs.note: Regular -er verb. Always check a dose against the prescription and the label.

example.target: Anne vérifie le sirop contre la toux.
example.native: Anne checks the cough syrup.

verbs.note: Regular -er verb. Nurses use vérifier or contrôler, not réviser.

example.target: M. Roux demande l'heure.
example.native: Mr. Roux asks the time.

verbs.note: Regular -er verb. It means to ask a question and also to ask someone to do something: demander à quelqu'un de faire.

lessons.title: Être: Who, How and Where
lessons.objective: Use être and se trouver to say who you are and describe a patient's condition and location.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Ask a patient if they are dizzy or tired, ask if they are allergic to any medication, and tell them where their family is.

items.note: étourdie for a woman. Ét- sounds like ay-: ay-toor-DEE.
fatiguée for a woman. Both sound the same: fa-tee-GAY.
éveillée for a woman. Same sound: ay-vay-YAY.
endormie for a woman. En- is nasal: ahn-dor-MEE.
Same form for a man and a woman. The final e is silent: kalm.
nerveuse for a woman. Final x is silent in the masculine: nehr-VUH.
Same form for a man and a woman. Before a noun, propre means own, so la plaie propre = the clean wound.
Use with être: il est allergique. Same form for a man and a woman. G before i sounds like zh and -que sounds like k: a-lehr-ZHEEK.
Plural in French: Les toilettes sont ici. For a room with a shower, la salle de bains.
Attente has a nasal an: sal da-TAHNT.
être for a profession, with no article: je suis infirmière. A man says je suis infirmier diplômé d'État.
French asks about dizziness with avoir: vous avez des vertiges. The adjective is étourdi: Vous êtes étourdi ? Ask a woman: Vous êtes étourdie ?

items.native: Are you allergic to any medication?
items.note: Être for a lasting trait. The inversion êtes-vous is polite; in speech Vous êtes allergique à un médicament ? is also fine.

items.target: Votre famille se trouve dans la salle d'attente.
items.native: Your family is in the waiting room.
items.note: se trouver for location. Everyday French often just says est: Votre famille est dans la salle d'attente.
Être links the wound and its condition. Plaie is feminine; propre has the same form for both genders.
Toilettes is plural, so the verb is sont.

passage.target: Anne : Bonjour, Monsieur Roux, je suis infirmière diplômée d'État.
passage.native: Anne: Good morning, Mr. Roux, I'm a registered nurse.

passage.target: M. Roux est éveillé, mais il est nerveux.
passage.native: Mr. Roux is awake, but he is nervous.

passage.target: Anne demande : Vous avez des vertiges ou vous êtes fatigué ?
passage.native: Anne asks: Are you dizzy or tired?

passage.target: M. Roux : Je n'ai pas de vertiges, mais je suis fatigué.
passage.native: Mr. Roux: I'm not dizzy, but I'm tired.
passage.note: Pas de replaces des after a negative: je n'ai pas de vertiges.

passage.target: Anne demande : Êtes-vous allergique à un médicament ?
passage.native: Anne asks: Are you allergic to any medication?

passage.target: M. Roux : Oui, je suis allergique à la pénicilline.
passage.native: Mr. Roux: Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin.

passage.target: Anne : Votre famille se trouve dans la salle d'attente.
passage.native: Anne: Your family is in the waiting room.

passage.target: Anne : La plaie est propre et les toilettes sont ici.
passage.native: Anne: The wound is clean and the bathroom is here.

passage.target: L'après-midi, M. Roux est calme et endormi.
passage.native: In the afternoon, Mr. Roux is calm and asleep.

verbs.native: to be (who or what someone is; how someone is)

example.target: Anne : Bonjour, Monsieur Roux, je suis infirmière diplômée d'État.
example.native: Anne: Good morning, Mr. Roux, I'm a registered nurse.

verbs.note: Irregular. French uses être for identity, job, lasting traits (je suis allergique) and conditions (je suis fatigué). With a patient use vous: Êtes-vous allergique ?

example.target: Anne : Votre famille se trouve dans la salle d'attente.
example.native: Anne: Your family is in the waiting room.

example.target: Anne demande : Êtes-vous allergique à un médicament ?
example.native: Anne asks: Are you allergic to any medication?

verbs.note: Regular -er verb. It means to ask a question and also to ask someone to do something.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask patients what they have, need or want, and say what has to be done.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Ask a patient if they have pain, nausea or thirst, and offer them water or a blanket.

items.note: In everyday speech, patients say avoir mal: j'ai mal. Ou is oo: doo-LUHR.
Plural in French too: j'ai des nausées. Stress the end: no-ZAY.
Say avoir de la fièvre: j'ai de la fièvre. One syllable, with an open è: FYEHVR.
avoir soif = to be thirsty, with no article. Oi sounds like wa; f is pronounced: swahf.
avoir faim = to be hungry, with no article. Aim is nasal: fan.
L'eau is feminine: de l'eau fraîche. Eau sounds like a plain o: lo.
Say it as koo-vehr-TUR. The u is the French u (lips rounded, say ee).
Nurses also say l'appel malade. Patients: sonner, to ring. Rhymes with net: so-NET.
Literally the hospital shirt. Not la blouse, which is a nurse's coat. Chemise: shuh-MEEZ.
The final ts is silent and an is nasal: gahn.
Avoir mal is how French says to have pain. To ask where: Où avez-vous mal ? Liaison: vooz-a-VAY mal.
Use vous with a patient. In speech you can also say Vous voulez une couverture ?

items.target: Il y a de l'eau sur la table.
items.note: Il y a = there is, there are. Run it together: eel-ya.

items.target: J'ai besoin de me laver les mains.
items.native: I need to wash my hands.
items.note: Avoir besoin de + infinitive. With body parts French uses the article: me laver les mains, not mes mains.

items.target: Selon la prescription, il faut prendre votre tension toutes les 4 heures.
items.native: Per the order, we have to take your blood pressure every 4 hours.
items.note: il faut + infinitive = it's necessary to. Toutes les 4 heures = every 4 hours.

passage.native: Nurse Anne visits Mr. Roux in the hospital.

example.target: Vous avez mal ?
example.native: Do you have pain?

example.target: J'ai besoin de me laver les mains.
example.native: I need to wash my hands.

example.target: Voulez-vous une couverture ?
example.native: Do you want a blanket?

example.native: Anne washes her hands.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell patients what you are going to do, what you do, and what they can do.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Tell a patient what you are going to do next: ask some questions, draw blood from the arm, and walk together in the hallway.

items.note: Short for la radiographie, the word patients and nurses use. Pronounced ra-DYO.
Nurses say le labo. Stress the end: la-bo-ra-TWAR.
Ch is sh and g before i is zh: shee-roor-ZHEE. Also the ward: le service de chirurgie.
Both syllables of sanguin are nasal and gu is a hard g: sahn-GAN. Also called l'analyse de sang.
Also means the act of drawing: faire un prélèvement. Stress the end: pray-lev-MAHN.
The s is silent: bra.
Ei sounds like eh: ven.
Ou is oo and oi is wa: koo-LWAR.
Ou is oo, ch is sh: doosh.
Not le sol, which is the floor you walk on. Le 3e étage = the 3rd floor.

items.target: Je vais vous faire une prise de sang au bras.
items.native: I'm going to draw blood from your arm.
items.note: Aller + infinitive tells what happens next. Prise de sang = blood draw. Nurses also say prélever du sang.

items.target: Je vais vous poser quelques questions.
items.native: I'm going to ask you some questions.
items.note: French says poser des questions (to put questions), not faire des questions.

items.target: On va marcher dans le couloir.
items.native: We're going to walk in the hallway.
items.note: On is the everyday we: on va = we're going. Nous allons is more formal.

items.target: À 10 h, on va vous faire une radio.
items.native: At 10 they're going to do an X-ray on you.
items.note: On va vous faire = they're going to do it on you. Say à dix heures.
Ask a woman: Pouvez-vous marcher seule ? Seul and seule sound the same: suhl.

example.native: I'm going to draw blood from your arm.

verbs.note: Irregular. Use aller + infinitive to tell a patient what is going to happen next: je vais, on va, ils vont.

example.target: Anne fait une prise de sang à M. Rameau.
example.native: Anne does a blood draw on Mr. Rameau.

example.target: Pouvez-vous marcher seul dans le couloir ?
example.native: Can you walk by yourself in the hallway?

verbs.note: Irregular, with a stem change: peux, peut, but pouvons, pouvez. Use the vous form pouvez with a patient. Seul for a man, seule for a woman.

example.target: Anne lui prélève du sang au bras.
example.native: Anne draws blood from his arm.

verbs.note: Regular -er verb with an accent change: the second e becomes è before a silent ending (prélève, prélèvent), but not in prélevons or prélevez. Prélever du sang is what nurses really say for drawing blood.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Describe daily shift routines in the present tense with patients and coworkers.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Talk with a coworker about your shift: when you work, who covers your patients at lunch, and when the doctors come by.

items.note: Je suis du matin = I'm on the morning shift. Poste de jour = day shift, poste de nuit = night shift. Pronounced post.
The first meal of the day. Pronounced puh-TEE day-zhuh-NAY.
In France déjeuner is lunch, not breakfast. Stress the end: day-zhuh-NAY.
The evening meal. The circumflex marks a lost s: dee-NAY.
Final -ment is nasal and the t is silent: may-dee-ka-MAHN.
La collègue for a woman. Both sound alike: ko-LEG.
The patient's chart is le dossier (de soins). Ss is s and final r is silent: do-SYAY.
Stress the last syllable: lor-dee-na-TUHR.
The doctors' rounds on the ward; it also means a visit. Pronounced vee-ZEET.
Poste de jour = day shift. Ill sounds like y: zhuh tra-VAHY duh ZHOOR.

items.target: Tu me remplaces auprès de mes patients à midi ?

items.note: Tu between colleagues. Remplacer = to cover for someone.

items.native: Do you eat well at home?
items.note: Vous with patients. In speech: Vous mangez bien chez vous ?
Ask a woman: Vivez-vous seule ?
In speech nurses say on regarde le dossier ensemble.
Passer = come by. The final -ent of passent is silent: pass.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask patients simple questions to verify identity and assess pain.
lessons.speakingPrompt: Verify a patient's name and date of birth, then ask where it hurts and how much pain they have from 0 to 10.

items.note: Quoi ends a sentence: Vous prenez quoi ? Before a subject use qu'est-ce que: Qu'est-ce que vous prenez ? Sounds kwa / kes-kuh.
Qu sounds like k: kee.
Où with an accent = where; ou without = or. Both sound oo.
Qu is k and an is nasal; the d is silent: kahn.
Combien de + noun: combien de comprimés ? Both om and ien are nasal: kohn-BYAN.
Use it before a noun, singular or plural: combien de comprimés ? De becomes d' before a vowel.
Ko-MAHN. Also what? if you did not hear.
Answer with parce que (two words) = because: poor-KWA.
Agrees with the noun: quel médicament, quelle dose. Both sound kel. Use quel/quelle + être for names, dates and numbers.
Formal, for patients. Liaison: vooz-a-play-VOO. Also Quel est votre nom ?

items.target: Quelle est votre date de naissance ?
items.native: What is your date of birth?
items.note: Quelle agrees with the feminine date.
Médecin traitant is the patient's regular doctor. Mayd-SAN.
Avoir mal = to hurt. Literally: where do you have pain?

items.target: De 0 à 10, vous avez mal à combien ?
items.native: From 0 to 10, how much pain do you have?
items.note: Say de zéro à dix. À combien = at what number, the everyday way nurses ask for a pain score. More formal: À combien évaluez-vous votre douleur ?

items.target: Quand êtes-vous allé à la selle pour la dernière fois ?
items.native: When was your last bowel movement?
items.note: Aller à la selle = to have a bowel movement. Ask a woman: êtes-vous allée. Patients often say aller aux toilettes.

passage.target: Anne : Bonjour, je suis votre infirmière, comment allez-vous ?
passage.native: Anne: Good morning, I am your nurse, how are you?

passage.target: Anne : Comment vous appelez-vous ?
passage.native: Anne: What is your name?

passage.target: Anne : Quelle est votre date de naissance ?
passage.native: Anne: What is your date of birth?

passage.target: Pierre : Pourquoi me posez-vous encore la question ?
passage.native: Pierre: Why are you asking again?

passage.target: Anne : C'est pour votre sécurité à l'hôpital.

items.note: Ne ... jamais wraps the verb: il ne dort jamais. In speech the ne often drops: il dort jamais. Pronounced zha-MEH.
Ne ... personne wraps the verb: je ne vois personne. Alone, it answers a question: Personne. Not the same as la personne (the person).
Ne ... rien wraps the verb: il ne mange rien. Alone: Rien. One nasal syllable: ryan.
Ne ... pas encore wraps the verb: ce n'est pas encore prêt. Alone: Pas encore.
At the end of a phrase the s is pronounced (plüs). In ne ... plus (no longer) it is silent.
Oin is a nasal sound and the s is silent: mwan.
Agrees with the noun: un autre verre, une autre couverture. Two words in French, unlike English another.

items.note: Patients say avoir mal. Pronounced doo-LUHR.

passage.target: Elle vérifie qu'il n'y a pas d'obstruction dans la tubulure et qu'elle n'est pas coudée.
